title: Gotama

teacherSummary.text: In the grove of Jetavana, Siddhartha and Govinda hear Gotama teach. Govinda joins the Buddha's followers. Siddhartha deeply admires Gotama but explains to him that enlightenment cannot be taught in words; each person must find it alone. Gotama warns him gently against too much cleverness, and Siddhartha leaves, feeling Gotama has taken his friend but given him himself.

items.prompt: State Siddhartha's main objection to following the Buddha, using this line. “nobody will obtain salvation by means of teachings!” (Gotama, paragraph 37) Answer by connecting it to one earlier chapter: quote a second passage and explain how the two passages together develop the idea.

Together the passages show his objection growing out of experience: no teacher, however great, has given anyone the self he seeks.

Exemplar: Siddhartha leaves the Buddha out of respect for the Buddha's own example. When the text says “Never before had Siddhartha venerated a person so much, never before had he loved a person as much as this one” (Gotama, paragraph 15), it shows this directly. Although he says he had never "venerated a person so much," he argues the Buddha reached enlightenment by his own search, so following any teaching, even this one, would betray that example.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.

items.text: Where do they hear Gotama teach?
items.lookFor: In the grove of Jetavana
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: In the grove of Jetavana near the town of Savathi, where the woman tells them the Buddha stays (Gotama, paragraph 4); the town is named in “In the town of Savathi, every child knew the name of the exalted Buddha” (Gotama, paragraph 1).

items.text: What does Govinda decide?
items.lookFor: To join Gotama's followers
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda takes his refuge in the Buddha and joins his monks: “I also take my refuge in the exalted one and his teachings” (Gotama, paragraph 19).

items.text: What does Siddhartha tell Gotama?
items.lookFor: Enlightenment cannot be taught in words
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: That the Buddha’s own enlightenment did not come from teachings and cannot be passed on in words. He says it to Gotama in Gotama, paragraph 37: “It has not come to you by means of teachings!” (Gotama, paragraph 37)

items.text: What does Gotama warn Siddhartha about?
items.lookFor: Being too clever
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: About too much cleverness: “Be aware of too much wisdom!” (Gotama, paragraph 42) (said with kindness, after praising him as wise).

items.text: How do the two Samanas find a place to sleep at the crowded Jetavana?
items.lookFor: Quickly and without any noise, as people used to the forest
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Being “accustomed to life in the forest,” they “found quickly and without making any noise a place to stay and rested there until the morning” (Gotama, paragraph 7).

items.text: Retell the three most important events of “Gotama” in order, in one sentence each.
items.lookFor: In the grove of Jetavana, Siddhartha and Govinda hear Gotama teach. Govinda joins the Buddha's followers. Siddhartha deeply admires Gotama but explains to him that enlightenment cannot be taught in words; each person must find it alone. Gotama warns him gently against too much cleverness, and Siddhartha leaves, feeling Gotama has taken his friend but given him himself.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: They find Gotama and hear him teach (Gotama, paragraphs 8–17); Govinda joins the monks and the friends part (paragraphs 19–24); Siddhartha tells the Buddha why he must go his own way and leaves (paragraphs 30–46).

items.text: Which characters appear or are mentioned in “Gotama”? Name two and one thing each says or does.
items.lookFor: Names and actions taken from the chapter; check against the teacher summary.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Two of: Gotama, who answers Siddhartha’s objection calmly (paragraph 36); Govinda, who takes refuge and weeps when he sees his friend will not (paragraphs 19, 24); the woman who directs them to Jetavana (paragraph 4).

items.text: Where and when does “Gotama” take place? Point to the line that tells you.
items.lookFor: A place/time detail quoted from the chapter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: In the town of Savathi and the grove of Jetavana, over one evening, night and morning. Time markers: “At sunrise, they saw with astonishment what a large crowd of believers and curious people had spent the night” (Gotama, paragraph 8)… and “Very early in the morning” (Gotama, paragraph 28).

items.text: Reread: “Quoth Siddhartha: ‘Yesterday, O exalted one, I had been privileged to hear your wondrous teachings.’” What does “privileged” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: privileged: given a special honour or chance.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Privileged” here means: given a special honour or chance. In Gotama, paragraph 31, Siddhartha opens his talk with Gotama by saying it was an honour to hear his teaching the day before.

items.text: Reread: “he exclaimed lamentingly.” What does “lamentingly” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: lamentingly: in a grieving, complaining way.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Lamentingly” here means: in a grieving, complaining way. In Gotama, paragraph 25, Govinda cries out in sorrow because Siddhartha will not join the Buddha’s monks with him.

items.text: What does “Gotama” suggest about the teacher and the teaching? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that admiring a teacher is not the same as following him) backed by one located line, such as the one in Gotama, paragraph 44.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests that admiring a teacher is not the same as following him. Support: “I have never before seen a person glance and smile, sit and walk this way, he thought” (Gotama, paragraph 44), yet he still leaves: what moves him is Gotama’s person, not the doctrine.

items.text: Find one example of characterization in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The Buddha is characterized by his walk and hand, not by praise: “The Buddha went on his way, modestly and deep in his thoughts, his calm face was neither happy nor sad” (Gotama, paragraph 12). It shows peace as something visible, which is exactly what Siddhartha wants to reach himself.

items.text: How does the theme in this chapter shape what we understand about the teacher and the teaching?
items.lookFor: Look for statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The theme that wisdom cannot be handed over shapes the parting: Siddhartha honours the teaching (paragraph 35) but refuses it for himself, “I wish that they shall all stay with the teachings” (Gotama, paragraph 40)… while he goes alone.

items.text: In the passage that begins “The Buddha went on his way, modestly and deep in his thoughts, his calm face was neither happy nor sad, it seemed to smile quietly and inwardly.”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In Gotama, paragraph 12, “modestly” and “calm” make holiness quiet and ordinary; the phrase “neither happy nor sad” shows a peace beyond moods.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Gotama”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: In the grove of Jetavana, Siddhartha and Govinda hear Gotama teach. Govinda joins the Buddha's followers. Siddhartha deeply admires Gotama but explains to him that enlightenment cannot be taught in words; each person must find it alone. Gotama warns him gently against too much cleverness, and…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The turn is Govinda joining the Buddha (paragraph 19), which forces Siddhartha to name his own choice (paragraphs 21–23). Effect: he is alone for the first time, which leads to the awakening in the next chapter.

items.text: How does “Gotama” build on “With the Samanas”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: the rumour of the Buddha in “With the Samanas” (paragraph 28) brings them to Jetavana; the doubt about all teaching that grew among the Samanas now makes Siddhartha refuse even the best teacher (paragraph 37).

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha says he leaves to find his own way, but his words also show pride; the Buddha senses it (“Be aware of too much wisdom!” (Gotama, paragraph 42)). Govinda claims conviction, but his tears in paragraph 24 show how much he depended on his friend.

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “Why does Siddhartha refuse to follow even a teacher he admires?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should go beyond ‘he is stubborn’ to his stated reason: salvation was not reached by the Buddha through teachings (Gotama, paragraph 37), so following teachings would repeat the Samanas’ mistake.

items.text: Where does conflict appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with the unity of all things?
items.lookFor: Look for the forces, people or desires pulling against each other.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The central conflict is Siddhartha’s respectful argument with Gotama (Gotama, paragraphs 35–37): the teaching describes the world as one unbroken chain, yet it breaks that unity by teaching overcoming it. That contradiction ties the chapter to the oneness he is seeking.

items.text: Background: Gotama is Siddhartha Gautama, the historical Buddha; Hesse deliberately gives his hero the Buddha's own name. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing that Gotama is the historical Buddha, and that the hero shares his name, makes the meeting a meeting with a double: Siddhartha must find for himself what the Buddha found, as he says in paragraph 37.

items.text: A critic might argue: “The parting of friends dramatizes the novel's thesis that wisdom must be lived, not adopted.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree: Govinda adopts a teaching (Gotama, paragraph 19) while Siddhartha leaves to live his way (paragraph 40). A text-based counterpoint: Siddhartha admits the teaching helps many (“it teaches many to live righteously, to avoid evil” (Gotama, paragraph 37)), so adopting it is not foolish for everyone.

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With humility as the standard, the Buddha is wisest: he answers without anger and wishes Siddhartha well (paragraphs 36, 39); Siddhartha, for all his insight, is closest to the pride Gotama warns about (paragraph 42). Other standards can reverse this.

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “Gotama” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about the teacher and the teaching?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda’s night after taking refuge (Gotama, paragraphs 24–27) works well: his view shows grief and loyalty but hides why Siddhartha will not join.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “Gotama”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘Where does Gotama teach?’ (Jetavana, paragraph 4); why/how, ‘Why does Siddhartha not join?’ (paragraph 37); what if, ‘Should Govinda have followed Siddhartha instead?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to teaching versus experience: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Strong: the chapter states the problem directly in Gotama, paragraph 37 (salvation does not come by teachings). Hesse now needs to show what experience teaches, which begins in “Awakening.”

items.text: Is the characterization in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective: Gotama is shown through gesture, smile and walk (paragraphs 12, 43), and Govinda’s grief is shown in tears (paragraph 24). A reviewer might find Siddhartha’s speech to the Buddha long and lecture-like (paragraphs 35–37).

items.text: Compare how “Gotama” treats the teacher and the teaching with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a student leaving a respected teacher or tradition and quote Siddhartha’s reason (paragraph 37); in this chapter the teacher is not wrong, which makes the parting harder than a simple rebellion.

items.text: Predict what “Awakening” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: Siddhartha has lost Govinda and refused all teachers (“He has deprived me of my friend” (Gotama, paragraph 46)), and he resolves to go his own way (paragraph 45). Prediction: alone, he will begin to look at himself and the world directly.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the teacher and the teaching?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps a student who meets a great mentor and friend, sees the friend join, and leaves to learn alone. What must stay is the reason in paragraph 37: what the mentor knows was not learned from a mentor.

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Is Siddhartha right to refuse the Buddha?’ The text gives both sides: he admires Gotama more than anyone (paragraph 44) but says no teaching can carry the experience (paragraph 37).

contentNotes.teacherNote: Teacher note on the portrait of Gotama: Hesse's Gotama is a European novelist's fictional portrait of the Buddha, not a historical record. The hero, Siddhartha, shares the historical Buddha's personal name (Siddhartha Gautama) but is a different, invented character; in the novel the two meet as separate people. The book is not a guide to Buddhist or Hindu teaching or practice, and Siddhartha's rejection of teachings (“nobody will obtain salvation by means of teachings!” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Gotama, para. 37)) is the character's view, not a verdict of Buddhism or Hinduism (Hesse, 1922/2001a; Müller, 1881/1999).
contentNotes.studentPreview: This chapter shows a novelist's imagined portrait of the Buddha.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “How is Hesse's Gotama different from the Buddha of history, and why does that matter?”
